why_how.text: A vehicle that is missing required equipment is unsafe and illegal, and a quick routine before each drive catches most problems.

scenario.text: Sam borrows his uncle's pickup, which has a front bumper but no rear bumper, only red reflectors at the back.

reasoning.text: A pickup or van may use reflectors in place of a rear bumper as long as it has a front bumper.

result.text: The pickup meets the bumper rule, so Sam adjusts his seat and mirrors, buckles up and drives.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking every vehicle must have both a front and a rear bumper.

correction.text: Private passenger cars need both, but pickups and vans may use reflectors instead of a rear bumper.

memory_support.text: Check, adjust, buckle; two brakes; horn only to avoid a crash.

prompt.text: Is honking to tell a friend you have arrived an acceptable use of the horn?

answer.text: No; use the horn to avoid a crash, never needlessly.

rationale.text: The manual says never to use the horn needlessly or to announce that you have arrived.

narration.text: Safe driving starts before the engine does. In this unit you will learn the simple routine the manual recommends before every drive, the equipment every car and truck must have, the bumper rules that differ between cars and pickups or vans, and the right and wrong ways to use the horn. Many of these items are exactly what an examiner checks before a road test, so they matter twice: once for your safety and once for your license. Think of this unit as a checklist you can run in less than a minute each time you get in.

Before driving on public roads, make sure the vehicle is fully equipped and in good condition, read the owner's manual, and regularly check the lights, wipers, horn and tires. When you get in, adjust your seat and mirrors, seat passengers where they do not block your view or interfere with your driving, and buckle up and have every passenger do the same. None of these steps takes long. A walk around the car and a glance at each light can reveal a problem before it becomes a crash or a ticket, and a properly adjusted seat and mirrors give you the best view of the road.

lines.text: Pickups and vans: front plus rear or reflectors

narration.text: Every car and truck must have at least two separate brake systems, such as the foot brake and the parking or emergency brake. The foot brake and the parking or emergency brake are the usual pair. Bumpers follow a rule that depends on the vehicle. Private passenger vehicles must have front and rear bumpers. Pickup trucks and vans need a front bumper plus either a rear bumper or reflectors. So a pickup with a front bumper and rear reflectors is legal, while a passenger car without a rear bumper is not. Keep that difference in mind when you look at any vehicle.

title.text: Reflectors only for pickups and vans

lines.text: Reflectors replace only a pickup or van rear bumper

narration.text: A common error is to treat the reflector option as if it applied to every vehicle. It does not. A private passenger car must have both a front and a rear bumper. Only a pickup truck or a van may use reflectors in place of a rear bumper, and only if it has a front bumper. If a question describes a sedan with rear reflectors but no rear bumper, that car does not meet the rule. If it describes a van or pickup with a front bumper and rear reflectors, it does. Read the vehicle type carefully before you decide whether the setup is allowed.

lines.text: Sirens and bells for emergencies only
Equipment list from wipers to taillights

narration.text: A vehicle must have a working horn, while bells, sirens and whistles are reserved for emergency vehicles. Use the horn to avoid a crash, never needlessly or to announce that you have arrived. The required equipment list also includes wipers, safety glass, a rearview mirror, license plates with a plate light, two ways to brake, high and low beam headlights, turn signals, bumpers, seat belts, a muffler, and a red taillight with red reflectors and a stop light. Each item on that list has a purpose, and the next units explain several of them in more detail.

Here is a quick check: you pull up outside a friend's house and want to let them know you have arrived. Is honking the horn an acceptable use? Recall the horn rule. A vehicle must have a working horn, and you use it to avoid a crash, never needlessly or to announce that you have arrived. So honking to signal your arrival is exactly the kind of use the manual tells you to avoid. Send a message or walk to the door instead, once you are parked. Save the horn for the moment it can actually prevent a collision with another driver or a pedestrian.

lines.text: Horn only to avoid a crash

narration.text: To sum up, before driving make sure the vehicle is fully equipped and in good condition, read the owner's manual, and check the lights, wipers, horn and tires regularly. Adjust your seat and mirrors, seat passengers so they do not block your view, and buckle everyone up. Every car and truck needs two separate brake systems. Cars need front and rear bumpers, while pickups and vans need a front bumper plus a rear bumper or reflectors. A working horn is required, sirens and bells are for emergency vehicles, and the horn is for avoiding a crash only. Next, you will look at headlights and lighting.

why_how.text: Lights let you see and be seen, and the manual gives exact distances and conditions for using them.

scenario.text: At four in the afternoon on a foggy day, Dana's car has its daytime running lights on, and she cannot see the road more than a few hundred feet ahead.

reasoning.text: Headlights must be on in fog or whenever you cannot see the road at least five hundred feet ahead, and daytime running lights do not turn on taillights.

result.text: Dana switches on her headlights so both front and rear lights are working.

claim.text: Common mistake: mixing up the three hundred fifty foot high beam distance with the five hundred foot visibility rule.

correction.text: High beams must show objects at least three hundred fifty feet ahead, while headlights must be on whenever you cannot see five hundred feet.

memory_support.text: High beams reach three fifty; headlights on when you cannot see five hundred.

prompt.text: Do daytime running lights turn on your taillights automatically?

answer.text: No; taillights and parking lights do not come on automatically.

rationale.text: Daytime running lights may switch on by themselves, but you still switch on headlights at sunset.

narration.text: Your vehicle's lights do two jobs. They help you see the road ahead, and they help everyone else see you. This unit covers the headlights and taillights every vehicle must have, how far high beams must reach, how to keep headlights working well, what daytime running lights do and do not do, the conditions that require headlights, and the plate light and turn signals. Two numbers in this unit are easy to confuse, three hundred fifty feet and five hundred feet, so the unit will show you how to keep them apart. Clear, working lights are part of being a safe driver.

lines.text: Two white headlights, high and low beam
Red taillights that light when braking
High beams reach three hundred fifty feet

narration.text: Every motor vehicle except a motorcycle needs two white headlights that work on both high and low beam, and red taillights that light up when the brake pedal is pressed. High beams must light up objects on the road at least three hundred fifty feet ahead. A white light must light the rear license plate so it can be seen at night, and every turn signal light on the vehicle must work. These are not optional extras. A burned-out plate light or turn signal means the vehicle is not properly equipped, so include them when you walk around the car to check its lights.

lines.text: Clean them as often as the windshield

narration.text: Damaged headlights must be replaced, because a cracked lens lets in moisture and dust that cut light output and add glare for other drivers. Dirty headlights can cut light output by as much as seventy-five percent, so clean them as often as you clean the windshield. Have the headlights inspected at least once a year to make sure they are aimed correctly. Damage, dirt and poor aim all reduce how well your headlights do their job. Clean, whole, well-aimed headlights give you the full distance the law expects from your high beams.

lines.text: Rain, snow, hail, sleet or fog
Can't see five hundred feet ahead

narration.text: Headlights go on at sunset and stay on until sunrise. They must also be on in rain, snow, hail, sleet or fog, or whenever you cannot see the road at least five hundred feet ahead. Daytime running lights may switch on automatically to make a vehicle more visible, but taillights and parking lights do not come on automatically. That means a car showing daytime running lights at dusk may have no lights at all at the back. Switch your headlights on yourself whenever any of these conditions applies, rather than trusting the car to do it for you.

lines.text: High beams: three hundred fifty feet
Headlights on: can't see five hundred

narration.text: Two different distances apply to headlights, and mixing them up is a classic error. High beams must show objects at least three hundred fifty feet ahead. That is about how far your lights must reach. Headlights must be on any time you cannot see the road for at least five hundred feet. That is about when you must use them. One number describes performance and the other describes a trigger. If a question asks how far high beams must reach, answer three hundred fifty. If it asks when headlights must be on because of poor visibility, the answer involves five hundred feet.

lines.text: Daytime running lights may be automatic
Taillights and parking lights are not

narration.text: Daytime running lights can turn on by themselves, but taillights and parking lights never do. So at sunset you still switch on your headlights. Many newer cars make this easy to forget, because the dashboard may look lit and the front of the car may glow even when the rear is dark. The rule is simple: when the sun goes down, when weather turns bad, or when you cannot see five hundred feet ahead, turn on the headlights. Doing so lights your taillights too, so drivers behind you can see you and know when you brake. Daytime running lights never replace that step.

Here is a quick check: your car's daytime running lights come on automatically when you start it. Does that mean your taillights are on as well? Think about what the manual says. Daytime running lights may switch on automatically to make the vehicle more visible, but taillights and parking lights do not come on automatically. So the answer is no. The rear of your car may be dark even though the front lights are glowing. At sunset, in bad weather, or whenever you cannot see five hundred feet ahead, switch on your headlights so the taillights light up too.

lines.text: Three hundred fifty and five hundred feet
Plate light and signals must work

narration.text: To recap, every motor vehicle except a motorcycle needs two white headlights with high and low beams and red taillights that light when you brake. High beams must reach at least three hundred fifty feet. Headlights go on from sunset to sunrise, in rain, snow, hail, sleet or fog, and whenever you cannot see five hundred feet ahead. Daytime running lights do not turn on the taillights. Replace damaged headlights, keep them clean because dirt can cut their output by up to seventy-five percent, and have their aim checked yearly. A white plate light and every turn signal must work too.

why_how.text: Some lights are reserved for special vehicles, and knowing who may use them helps you read the road.
Mirrors, mufflers and belts protect you and everyone around you.

scenario.text: A tow truck pulls up to a crash scene showing amber flashing lights, and a rural mail carrier nearby shows a strobe lamp.

reasoning.text: Tow trucks may use flashing lights but not blue lights, and rural mail carriers may use strobe lamps but are not on the flashing-light list.

result.text: Both vehicles are using lights they are allowed to use.

claim.text: Common mistake: believing airbags make seat belts unnecessary.

correction.text: Airbags work together with seat belts but do not keep occupants from being thrown out, and Minnesota requires everyone to wear a belt.

memory_support.text: Blue for plows and emergencies, flash for helpers, strobe for buses, snow and mail.

prompt.text: Is a tow truck allowed to show blue lights at a crash scene?

answer.text: No; blue lights are limited to snowplows, road maintenance equipment and authorized emergency vehicles.

rationale.text: Tow trucks are on the flashing-light list but not the blue-light list.

narration.text: This unit covers equipment that protects people or tells you something about other vehicles. First come the three kinds of special lights: blue lights, flashing lights and strobe lamps, each limited to certain vehicles. Then you will learn why every vehicle needs a muffler and what to check it for, which mirrors are required, and the seat belt and airbag rules. The light lists overlap in places, so the unit will point out exactly where they differ. Knowing them helps you recognize emergency and service vehicles and avoid using lights your own car is not allowed to have.

lines.text: Flashing: longer list incl. tow trucks
Strobes: buses, snow removal, mail carriers

narration.text: Blue lights are limited to snowplows, road maintenance equipment and authorized emergency vehicles. Flashing lights are limited to tow trucks, school buses, farm equipment, service vehicles, road maintenance equipment and authorized emergency vehicles. Strobe lamps are limited to school buses, snow removal equipment and rural mail carrier vehicles. An ordinary passenger car is on none of these lists. So if you see blue lights, think plow, road crew or emergency vehicle. If you see flashing lights, the vehicle could be one of several helpers. If you see a strobe, think school bus, snow removal or a rural mail carrier.

lines.text: Tow trucks flash but never blue

narration.text: The three lists overlap, and that is where mistakes happen. Blue lights belong only to snowplows, road maintenance equipment and emergency vehicles, while tow trucks, service vehicles and farm equipment may show flashing lights but not blue ones. School buses may use both flashing lights and strobe lamps. Rural mail carrier vehicles may use strobe lamps, but they are not on the flashing-light list. When a question names a vehicle and a light, check the vehicle against the right list. A tow truck with blue lights, for example, is not following the rule, even though tow trucks may flash.

lines.text: Check it for carbon monoxide leaks
Rearview mirror, plus side mirror when needed

narration.text: Every motor vehicle needs a muffler to prevent sudden or prolonged loud noise such as popping or crackling, and the muffler should be checked regularly for carbon monoxide leaks. Passenger vehicles need rearview mirrors. A vehicle with no view through a rear window, such as a rental moving truck, or a pickup used for hauling, needs an extra side mirror as well. If you rent a moving truck or load a pickup so high that you cannot see out the back, make sure the side mirrors are in place and adjusted before you set off, since the rearview mirror alone will not show you what is behind.

Minnesota requires seat belts in all vehicles and requires everyone to wear them, and belts should be kept clean and in good condition for all occupants. Airbags work together with seat belts, but they do not keep occupants from being thrown out of the vehicle. A cluttered dashboard can also turn objects into hazards when airbags inflate, because anything sitting there may be thrown toward the people inside. Keep the dashboard clear, make sure every belt latches and retracts properly, and remember that the belt, not the airbag, is what keeps you in your seat.

Here is a quick check: a tow truck arrives at a stalled car on the highway. May the tow truck use blue lights? Think about the three lists. Blue lights are limited to snowplows, road maintenance equipment and authorized emergency vehicles. Flashing lights are allowed for tow trucks, school buses, farm equipment, service vehicles, road maintenance equipment and emergency vehicles. So the tow truck may use flashing lights, but blue lights are not allowed for it. Remembering that tow trucks flash but never show blue is one of the simplest ways to sort these lists correctly.

To finish, blue lights are only for snowplows, road maintenance equipment and emergency vehicles. Flashing lights cover those plus tow trucks, school buses, farm equipment and service vehicles. Strobe lamps are for school buses, snow removal equipment and rural mail carriers, and mail carriers are not on the flashing list. Every vehicle needs a muffler checked for carbon monoxide leaks. Passenger vehicles need rearview mirrors, with an extra side mirror for hauling pickups or vehicles with no rear view. Everyone must wear a seat belt, and airbags work with belts but cannot prevent ejection.

why_how.text: Tires are your only contact with the road, so pressure and tread decide how well you grip, steer and stop.

scenario.text: Jae wants to top up his tires right after a long drive and reads the number molded on the tire sidewall as the target.

reasoning.text: The recommended pressure is on the door sticker or in the owner's manual, and pressure is checked before driving or at least three hours after driving.

result.text: Jae waits three hours, reads the door sticker and adjusts each tire to that number.

claim.text: Common mistake: using the number printed on the tire sidewall as your target pressure.

correction.text: The target is on the sticker inside the driver's door or in the owner's manual, not the sidewall.

memory_support.text: Door sticker sets the target, check cold, one-sixteenth or Lincoln decides.

prompt.text: You place a penny into the shallowest groove and the tread covers part of Lincoln's head. Is the tire legal?

answer.text: Yes; tread covering any part of his head means the tire is legal and safe.

rationale.text: The penny test checks the one-sixteenth inch legal limit.

narration.text: Everything your car does, from steering to stopping, depends on four small patches of rubber touching the road. This unit covers how to look over your tires, why loose surfaces reduce grip, how quickly tires lose pressure, where to find the correct pressure and when to measure it, the legal limit for tread depth, and the penny test you can do in a driveway. Two traps wait in this unit. One is the number on the tire sidewall, and the other is checking pressure at the wrong time. You will learn how to avoid both. Small checks make a big difference.

Look over your tires often for bulges, punctures, bald spots, cuts, cracks or uneven wear, and carry a good spare whose pressure you also check often. Be aware that tires grip gravel or dirt roads less well than concrete or asphalt, so the same tire that feels secure on pavement may slide more easily on a gravel road. A careful look at each tire takes only a minute when you walk around the car. Catching a bulge or a cut early can prevent a sudden failure, and a properly inflated spare means a flat tire is an inconvenience rather than an emergency.

title.text: Pressure and where to find it

lines.text: Use the door sticker or owner's manual

narration.text: A tire can lose up to one pound per square inch of pressure a month, so check pressure often and never drive on under-inflated tires. The recommended tire pressure is on a sticker inside the driver's door or in the owner's manual. It is not the number printed on the tire sidewall. Check tire pressure before driving or at least three hours after driving, then add or release air until the gauge matches the recommended number. Following that routine each month keeps the tires at the pressure the vehicle maker intended, which helps grip and also, as a later unit explains, saves fuel.

lines.text: Sidewall number is not the target
Do not check right after a trip

narration.text: Two habits lead drivers astray. The first is reading the number on the tire sidewall and filling the tire to it. The tire pressure to aim for is the one on the driver's door sticker or in the owner's manual, while the sidewall number is not the target. The second is checking pressure right after a drive. Tire pressure is checked either before you drive or only once at least three hours have passed since driving, not right after a trip. Get both habits right and your gauge reading will match the pressure the vehicle actually needs.

lines.text: Less than one-sixteenth inch is illegal

narration.text: Tread is the grooved rubber that grips the road. A tire is illegal when its tread is less than one-sixteenth of an inch deep. That is not much depth, so a tire close to the limit is already worn. You can measure tread with a gauge, but the manual also describes a quick check that uses a coin you probably have in your pocket. Whatever method you use, check the shallowest part of each tire, because tires do not always wear evenly. Uneven wear is one of the warning signs the manual tells you to watch for when you inspect your tires.

lines.text: Lincoln's head into the shallowest groove
Tread covers part of his head: legal

narration.text: In the penny test, you place Lincoln's head into the shallowest tread groove. If the tread covers any part of his head, the tire is legal and safe. If you can see the whole of his head, the tread is too shallow. The legal tread limit is one-sixteenth of an inch, and the penny test passes only when tread covers part of Lincoln's head. It is a quick way to check the same limit without special tools. Do the test in more than one spot on each tire, and if any spot fails, plan to replace the tire before you drive much farther.

lines.text: Tread covers part of Lincoln's head

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you place a penny into the shallowest groove of a tire, and the tread covers part of Lincoln's head. Is the tire legal? Remember how the penny test works. You put Lincoln's head into the shallowest groove, and if the tread covers any part of his head, the tire is legal and safe. So the answer is yes. The penny test is simply a quick way to check the legal limit of one-sixteenth of an inch. If you could see all of Lincoln's head instead, the tread would be too shallow and the tire would need replacing.

lines.text: Inspect often, carry a good spare
One-sixteenth inch and the penny test

narration.text: To wrap up, look over your tires often for bulges, punctures, bald spots, cuts, cracks or uneven wear, and keep a good spare. Remember that tires grip gravel and dirt less well than pavement. A tire can lose up to one pound per square inch a month, so check pressure often, using the number on the door sticker or in the owner's manual rather than the sidewall, and measure before driving or three hours after. Tread less than one-sixteenth of an inch is illegal, and the penny test passes when tread covers part of Lincoln's head.

why_how.text: A clear view through every window is a legal requirement, and the tint and windshield rules are specific.

scenario.text: Lee wants to hang a small air freshener from the rearview mirror and add a toll device to the windshield.

reasoning.text: Toll devices allowed by state law may go on the windshield, but nothing may hang between the driver and the windshield.

result.text: Lee mounts the toll device on the windshield and puts the air freshener somewhere else.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking dark tint is fine on any window as long as it is labeled.

correction.text: Tint transmitting under fifty percent or reflecting over twenty percent is allowed only on a pickup's rear window or the rear and side windows of a van, limousine or funeral home vehicle.

memory_support.text: Stick legal items on, hang nothing, keep dark tint to the back of special vehicles.

prompt.text: May a windshield be covered with a film that makes it more reflective?

answer.text: No; a windshield may not be covered or treated with material that makes it more reflective or lets less light through.

rationale.text: The darker and reflective tint allowances apply only to certain rear and side windows, never the windshield.

lines.text: What may go on the glass

narration.text: You cannot avoid what you cannot see, so the manual is strict about glass. This unit covers what must not block your view, which stickers and devices may go on the windshield, what may never be done to a windshield, how side and rear window tint must be labeled, how dark or reflective tint is limited to certain vehicles, and the wiper, defroster and fender rules. Many of these points come up when you buy or modify a car, so knowing them can save you a ticket and help you keep the clear view the law requires. Clear glass is a legal requirement, not a preference.

lines.text: Nothing hanging in front of you

narration.text: The view through the windshield and windows must not be blocked by cracks, discoloration, steam, frost, ice or snow, and nothing may hang between the driver and the windshield. A vehicle with a glass windshield must have working wipers, and defrosters are needed to keep the windshield and windows free of steam and frost. On a cold morning that means clearing every window, not just a small patch in front of you, and giving the defroster time to work before you pull out. Wipers that smear or skip should be replaced so rain and snow do not block your view either.

title.text: What may go on the windshield

lines.text: Navigation low, monitors near the mirror

narration.text: Some items may go on the windshield. Stickers allowed by state law, such as park stickers and safety inspection stickers, and toll devices may be placed there. Navigation units may mount near the bottom of the windshield, and driver monitoring equipment may sit just behind, above or below the rearview mirror. What is not allowed is anything hanging between the driver and the windshield. So a toll device stuck to the glass is fine, while an object dangling from the mirror is not. The idea is that permitted items sit in places that do not block your main line of sight.

lines.text: Windshield: never more reflective or darker
Tint after nineteen eighty-five must be labeled
Dark tint limited to certain vehicles

narration.text: A windshield may not be made of, covered with or treated with any material that makes it more reflective or lets less light through. Side or rear window tint applied after August first, nineteen eighty-five must be labeled with the percentage of light it transmits and reflects. Tint that transmits less than fifty percent or reflects more than twenty percent of light is allowed only on a pickup's rear window or on the rear and side windows of a van, limousine or funeral home vehicle. So an ordinary car may not carry tint that dark on its windows, and no vehicle may darken its windshield.

The two tint numbers are easy to swap. Dark tint that lets through less than fifty percent of light, or reflects more than twenty percent, is limited to pickup rear windows and to the rear and side windows of vans, limousines and funeral home vehicles, never the windshield. Fifty goes with how much light passes through, and twenty goes with how much is reflected. If a question swaps them, the answer is wrong. Also notice that a label does not make dark tint legal on an ordinary car. The label is required, but the vehicle and window must also be on the allowed list.

Here is a quick check: a driver wants to cover the windshield with a film that makes it more reflective. Is that allowed? Recall the windshield rule. A windshield may not be made of, covered with or treated with any material that makes it more reflective or lets less light through. So the answer is no. The allowances for dark or reflective tint apply only to a pickup's rear window and to the rear and side windows of vans, limousines and funeral home vehicles, never to the windshield. The windshield must stay as clear as possible so the driver can see the road ahead.

lines.text: Legal stickers and toll devices allowed
Dark tint only where allowed; fenders

narration.text: To recap, the view through every window must not be blocked by cracks, discoloration, steam, frost, ice or snow, and nothing may hang between you and the windshield. Legal stickers and toll devices may go on the windshield, navigation units near its bottom and monitoring equipment near the mirror. The windshield may never be made more reflective or darker. Tint after the nineteen eighty-five cutoff must be labeled, and tint under fifty percent transmission or over twenty percent reflection is limited to certain rear and side windows. Wipers and defrosters must work, and passenger vehicles need fenders or wheel guards so tires do not throw debris.

why_how.text: Small habits in how you maintain and drive your vehicle add up to real fuel savings.

scenario.text: Maria runs three errands on three separate trips each Saturday, accelerating hard from every stop.

reasoning.text: Driving efficiently means combining errands and avoiding hard acceleration and sudden braking.

result.text: Maria plans one combined route and starts and stops smoothly, using less fuel.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking fuel use depends only on the car, not on how you drive or travel.

correction.text: Combining errands, smooth driving, removing heavy items and choosing shared or active travel all save fuel.

memory_support.text: Tune, inflate, oil; combine, smooth, steady; share or walk.

prompt.text: Which maintenance steps help a vehicle use less fuel?

answer.text: Keeping the engine tuned, the tires properly inflated and the recommended grade of oil in the engine.

rationale.text: The manual lists these three maintenance habits as fuel savers.

narration.text: The last part of the vehicle chapter turns from safety equipment to efficiency. Fuel costs money, and how you care for and drive your vehicle changes how much you use. This short unit covers three areas: the maintenance that keeps an engine efficient, the driving habits that waste or save fuel, and the travel choices that can replace a car trip altogether. These tips are recommendations rather than laws, but several of them overlap with safe driving, such as obeying the speed limit and avoiding sudden braking, so they are worth building into your routine from day one.

Save fuel by keeping the engine tuned, keeping the tires properly inflated and using the recommended grade of motor oil in the engine. Each of these is part of ordinary maintenance. None of them needs special skill, only regular attention to the vehicle. Tire pressure links back to the earlier unit on tires: checking pressure often and filling to the number on the door sticker or in the owner's manual not only helps grip and safety but also keeps your fuel use down. Good care pays off in more than one way, and it takes very little time.

lines.text: Avoid speeding, hard starts, sudden stops
Remove extra weight; cruise on highways

narration.text: Drive efficiently by combining errands, avoiding speeding, hard acceleration and sudden braking, obeying the speed limit, removing heavy items you do not need, and using cruise control and overdrive on the highway. Notice how many of these are also safety habits. Obeying the speed limit is also the law. Planning one route for several errands means fewer cold starts and fewer miles. Clearing heavy items out of the trunk lightens the load. On the highway, cruise control and overdrive help keep a steady, efficient speed.

title.text: It is not only the car

lines.text: How you drive changes fuel use
How you travel changes it too

narration.text: A common belief is that fuel use is fixed by the car you own. The manual shows otherwise. The same car uses more fuel when it is driven with hard acceleration, sudden braking and speeding, or when it carries heavy items you do not need, and less when you combine errands and drive smoothly. Travel choices matter as well. Public transportation, carpools, ridesharing, biking or walking are recommended whenever possible to save fuel. So the driver and the trip plan are just as important as the vehicle. Small changes to both add up over a year of driving.

Here is a quick check: which maintenance steps does the manual list for saving fuel? Think back to the first part of this unit. The manual says to keep the engine tuned, keep the tires properly inflated and use the recommended grade of motor oil in the engine. Those three habits are part of ordinary vehicle care. Add the driving habits, such as combining errands and avoiding hard acceleration, and the travel choices, such as carpooling or walking, and you have the full picture. Each of these choices is simple, and each one helps you use less fuel over a year of driving.

To finish, keep the engine tuned, the tires properly inflated and the recommended grade of motor oil in the engine. Drive efficiently by combining errands, avoiding speeding, hard acceleration and sudden braking, obeying the speed limit, removing heavy items you do not need, and using cruise control and overdrive on the highway. Whenever you can, use public transportation, carpools, ridesharing, biking or walking instead of driving. That wraps up the vehicle chapter: a properly equipped, well-maintained vehicle, driven smoothly, is both safer and cheaper to run.
